en: Thus have I heard— The Discourse on the Great Simile of the Heartwood (Mahāsāropamasutta), the twenty-ninth in the Middle Collection (Majjhima Nikāya).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.
There, concerning Devadatta, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"In this case, bhikkhus, a certain son of good family, out of faith, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, thinking: [‘...’]"
“I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
Having gone forth thus, he nevertheless generates gain, honor, and fame.
He becomes elated by that gain, honor, and renown, his purpose fulfilled.
On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
“I possess gain, honor, and renown, whereas these other bhikkhus are unknown and of little influence.”
Thus, through that gain, honor, and fame, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

Just as if, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass by a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the bark, and passing over...
Having cut off the bark, the sapwood, and the foliage, he would take it and depart, thinking, "This is the heartwood.
A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say:
"Truly, this worthy man did not know the heartwood; he did not know the sapwood; he did not know the bark; he did not know the inner bark; he did not know the foliage."
In the same way, this man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passed by the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood;
passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the bark, and passing over the inner bark, he cut off branches and foliage,
took them away, and departed, thinking they were "heartwood."
‘And whatever purpose he has to accomplish with its heartwood, that purpose it will not fulfill.
In the same way, monks, here a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.’
‘Perhaps an end might be discerned to this entire mass of suffering.
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and fame.
He becomes elated by that gain, honor, and fame, his purpose fulfilled.

Thus, by means of that gain, honor, and renown, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking: "I possess gain, honor, and renown, whereas these other bhikkhus are unknown and of little influence.
He becomes intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he becomes negligent and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.
This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who has grasped the branches and foliage of the holy life.
And by that, he reaches a state of rest.
But here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering."
‘Perhaps an end might be made to this entire mass of suffering.
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and renown.
Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he is not satisfied and his purpose is not fulfilled.
Thus, because of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and fame; he is not negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness.
Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtuous conduct.
Thus, being satisfied with that perfection of virtue, his intention is fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am virtuous and of beautiful character, but these other bhikkhus are immoral and of evil character."
Thus, through that perfection of virtue, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

Just as if, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass right by the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, passing by the sapwood, and passing by the bark—
Having cut off the outer bark and taken it away, he would depart thinking, "This is the heartwood.
A man with good eyesight, seeing him, would say:

"Truly, this person did not recognize the heartwood; he did not recognize the sapwood; he did not recognize the inner bark; he did not recognize the outer bark; he did not recognize the twigs and leaves."
In the same way, this man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
passed right by the heartwood of a large standing tree possessed of heartwood, passed by the sapwood, and passed by the bark; having cut off the outer shell,
he took it and departed, thinking, "This is heartwood."
‘Whatever must be accomplished with its core, that purpose it will not achieve.
In the same way, monks, here a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.’
‘Perhaps an end might be discerned to this entire mass of suffering.
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and renown.
Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he is not satisfied and his purpose is not fulfilled.
Thus, because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he is not negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness.
Being heedful, he achieves perfection in virtuous conduct.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of virtue and his intention is fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am virtuous and of beautiful character, whereas these other bhikkhus are immoral and of evil character."
Thus, through that perfection of virtue, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.
This, monks, is called a monk who has grasped the outer bark of the holy life and has thereby reached a point of rest.
But here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be made known."
Having thus gone forth, he generates gain, honor, and renown.
He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and renown, nor does his aspiration reach fulfillment.
Because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
Thus, he is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and fame; he does not become negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Because of that perfection in virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
Thus, through that perfection of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness.
Being heedful, he achieves perfection in concentration.
Through that perfection of concentration, he becomes elated and his aspirations are fulfilled.
Thus, on account of that perfection of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am concentrated, with a one-pointed mind, whereas these other bhikkhus are unconcentrated and have wandering minds.
Through that perfection of concentration, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.
“Just as if, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by a great tree standing possessed of heartwood; and having bypassed the heartwood and the sapwood, he were to cut off the bark and take it away,
thinking, ‘This is heartwood.’”

A man with good eyesight, seeing this, would say: "Truly, this worthy man did not recognize the heartwood; he did not recognize the sapwood; he did not recognize the bark; he did not recognize the inner bark; he did not recognize the twigs and leaves.

For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, has passed right by the heartwood of this great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and having cut off the bark, he has taken it and departed."
“Thinking, ‘This is the core,’ yet he will not experience that purpose which is to be accomplished by means of the core.
In the same way, monks, here a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, [thinking]: [“I am one who has gone forth for the sake of the core.”]
“I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
Having gone forth in this way, he nevertheless generates gain, honor, and renown.
Thus, he is not elated by that gain, honor, and renown, nor does his intention become fulfilled thereby.
He does not exalt himself because of that gain, honor, and renown, nor does he disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he does not become negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of virtue, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He does not become intoxicated by that perfection of virtue, nor negligent, nor fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he achieves the perfection of concentration.
Thus, being satisfied with that perfection of concentration, his intention is fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of concentration, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I am concentrated, my mind is one-pointed; but these other bhikkhus are unconcentrated, their minds are distracted."
Thus, through that perfection of concentration, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness. Being heedless, he dwells in suffering.
This, monks, is called a monk who has grasped the outer bark of the holy life and has reached his limit with that.
But here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; overcome by suffering, beset by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be made known."
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and renown.
He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and renown, nor does his aspiration reach fulfillment through it.
On account of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
Thus, he is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he does not become negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness.
Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, because of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
Because of that perfection of virtue, he is not intoxicated, he is not negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he achieves perfection of concentration.
Because of that perfection of concentration, he is satisfied, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, because of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that perfection of concentration, he is not negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision.
Through that knowledge and vision, he becomes satisfied and his purpose is fulfilled.
Thus, by means of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others,
thinking: "I dwell knowing and seeing,
but these other bhikkhus dwell unknowing and unseeing."
Thus, through that knowledge and vision, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.

Just as if, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass right by a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, and having cut away the sapwood, were to take it and depart, thinking, "This is heartwood."
A man with sight, seeing this, would say:
"Truly, this worthy man did not know the heartwood, he did not know the sapwood, he did not know the bark, he did not know the inner bark, and he did not know the twigs and leaves.

For this worthy man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passed right by the heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood; instead, having cut off the sapwood, he has taken it and departed, thinking, 'This is heartwood.'"
‘And whatever must be done with its heartwood, that purpose it will not fulfill.
In the same way, monks, here a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.’
‘Perhaps an end might be discerned to this entire mass of suffering.
Having thus gone forth, he brings about gain, honor, and fame.
Because of that gain, honor, and fame, he is not satisfied and his purpose is not fulfilled.
Thus, because of that gain, honor, and renown, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he is not negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his aspiration is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, because of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
Because of that perfection of virtue, he is not intoxicated, he is not negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he achieves perfection of concentration.
Because of that perfection of concentration, he is satisfied, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Thus, because of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that perfection of concentration, he is not negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision.
Being satisfied with that knowledge and vision, his aspirations are fulfilled.
Thus, by means of that knowledge and vision, he exalts himself and disparages others, thinking:
"I dwell knowing and seeing, but these other bhikkhus dwell unknowing and unseeing.
Through that knowledge and vision, he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, and falls into heedlessness; being heedless, he dwells in suffering.
“Monks, this is called a monk who has grasped the softwood of the holy life and has reached a stopping point with it. But here, monks,
a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:”
“I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.
Having thus gone forth, he nevertheless generates gain, honor, and fame.
Thus, he is not elated by that gain, honor, and fame, nor does his intention become fulfilled thereby.
He does not exalt himself because of that gain, honor, and fame, nor does he disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and fame; he does not become negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of virtue, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He does not become intoxicated by that perfection of virtue, nor negligent, nor fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he achieves the perfection of concentration.
Thus, he is satisfied with that perfection of concentration, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that perfection of concentration; he is not negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision.
Thus he is satisfied with that knowledge and vision, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Through that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
He is not intoxicated by that knowledge and vision, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being diligent, he attains liberation at any time.
"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question that such a monk should fall away from that liberation not subject to time.

Just as if, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to cut down the very heartwood of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood and, knowing it to be 'heartwood,' take it and depart;
and a man with sight, seeing him, were to say this:"
‘This worthy man has indeed recognized the heartwood, he has recognized the sapwood, he has recognized the bark, he has recognized the inner bark, and he has recognized the twigs and leaves.

For this worthy man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, having cut down the very heartwood of that great standing tree possessed of heartwood, has taken it and departed, knowing it to be “heartwood.
Whatever purpose there may be to be served by heartwood, he will experience that benefit.’”
In the same way, monks, here a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs; immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be made known."
Having thus gone forth, he produces gain, honor, and fame.
He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and fame, nor does his intention become fulfilled by it.
On account of that gain, honor, and fame, he does not exalt himself or disparage others.
Thus, he is not intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he does not become negligent, nor does he fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, he achieves perfection in virtue.
He is satisfied with that perfection in virtue, yet his purpose is not yet fulfilled.
On account of that perfection in virtue, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
Thus, through that perfection of virtue, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being heedful, he achieves perfection of concentration.
Through that perfection of concentration, he becomes satisfied, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Through that perfection of concentration, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.
Thus, through that perfection of concentration, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness; being heedful, he achieves knowledge and vision.
He is satisfied with that knowledge and vision, yet his intention is not yet fulfilled.
Through that knowledge and vision, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others.

Thus, by means of that knowledge and vision, he does not become intoxicated, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into heedlessness. Being heedful, he attains liberation that is not occasional.
Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that such a monk should fall away from that non-occasional liberation.

Thus, monks, this holy life does not have gain, honor, and renown as its benefit; nor does it have the perfection of virtue as its benefit; nor does it have the perfection of concentration as its benefit; nor does it have knowledge and vision as its benefit.
"But as for this unshakable liberation of mind, monks,
this is the purpose of the holy life, this is its essence, this is its culmination.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The ninth discourse, the Mahāsāropama Sutta, is finished.
